rationale: A wins because its best angle is a real assignment, not a launch note: "Khan Academy's AI tutor reaches 1 million more students before the research is in" gives an education-evidence reporter conflict, timing, and the proof hurdle. B is disciplined, but "Donors, not districts, are paying for the AI tutor headed to 1 million more students" states a payment fact the update does not actually give, then asks later whether districts pay. A has its own market-contrast overreach, but its reporter shapes and proof gates are sharper across the set.
gaps_in_A: "A donor-funded nonprofit is giving away AI tutoring that competitors sell" imports a competitor-pricing frame the update never supplied.
"the same capability is a paid product elsewhere" repeats the unsupported market claim inside the angle body.
"How Khanmigo helps teachers save time on lesson planning" is refused as "duplicate," but "save time" is also an unsupported benefit claim; the cleaner refusal is hallucinated_fact.
gaps_in_B: "Donors, not districts, are paying for the AI tutor headed to 1 million more students" overclaims. The update says free to teachers and donor-funded, not that districts pay nothing.
"Its own study is the first test of that claim" stretches "first classroom results" into a broader exclusivity claim it cannot prove from the supplied facts.
"a data desk at a national outlet" is a bit grand for an internal, non-peer-reviewed edtech efficacy study; the trade/education-research target is the real lane.
"Khan Academy transforms K-12 learning with AI" — `slop` is true but lazy. The refusal should name the false outcome claim, not just slap a label on it.
